arrays.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array by its index?
arrays.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, so any index can be computed directly from the base address in constant time.

arrays.question: What happens when you insert an element at the beginning of an array of size n?

choices.B: All n elements must shift right

arrays.explanation: Inserting at position 0 requires shifting all existing elements one position to the right, making it an O(n) operation.

arrays.question: Which property distinguishes arrays from linked lists?

choices.C: Arrays have dynamic size by default
choices.D: Arrays store elements in non-sequential memory

arrays.explanation: Arrays allocate a contiguous block of memory, enabling O(1) random access, whereas linked lists use scattered nodes connected by pointers.

arrays.question: An array has indices 0 through 9. What is the index of the 7th element?
arrays.explanation: Arrays use zero-based indexing, so the 7th element is at index 6.

linked_lists.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list?
linked_lists.explanation: Inserting at the head only requires creating a new node and updating the head pointer — no shifting needed.

linked_lists.question: What is the main disadvantage of a singly linked list compared to an array?

choices.B: No random access — must traverse sequentially

linked_lists.explanation: Linked lists lack contiguous memory, so accessing the kth element requires traversing k nodes from the head.

linked_lists.question: In a doubly linked list, each node contains:

choices.C: Data and two pointers (next and previous)
choices.D: Two data fields and one pointer

linked_lists.explanation: A doubly linked list node holds data, a pointer to the next node, and a pointer to the previous node, enabling traversal in both directions.

linked_lists.question: To delete a node from the middle of a singly linked list, you need:

choices.A: Access to the node to delete only
choices.B: Access to the node before the one to delete
choices.D: The index of the node in an array

linked_lists.explanation: In a singly linked list, you must update the previous node's next pointer to skip the deleted node, so you need access to the predecessor.

stacks.question: Which principle does a stack follow?
stacks.explanation: A stack follows Last-In-First-Out: the most recently pushed element is the first to be popped.

stacks.question: If you push A, B, C onto a stack (in that order), what is the first element popped?
stacks.explanation: C was pushed last, so under LIFO it is popped first.

stacks.question: Which real-world application commonly uses a stack?
stacks.explanation: Undo operations reverse the most recent action first, which matches LIFO behavior — a perfect use case for stacks.

stacks.question: What operation retrieves the top element without removing it?
stacks.explanation: Peek (or top) returns the element at the top of the stack without modifying the stack.

queues.question: Which principle does a queue follow?
queues.explanation: A queue follows First-In-First-Out: the element added first is removed first.

queues.question: If you enqueue 10, 20, 30 (in that order), what does dequeue return?
queues.explanation: 10 was enqueued first, so under FIFO it is dequeued first.

queues.question: A circular queue solves which problem of a linear array-based queue?

choices.B: Wasted space at the front after dequeues

queues.explanation: In a linear array queue, dequeuing wastes front slots. A circular queue wraps around, reusing freed space.

queues.question: Which traversal algorithm primarily uses a queue?
queues.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level, using a queue to track which nodes to visit next.

recursion.question: Every recursive function must have:
recursion.explanation: Without a base case the function calls itself infinitely, causing a stack overflow. The base case provides the termination condition.

recursion.question: What data structure does the system use to manage recursive function calls?
recursion.explanation: Each recursive call is pushed onto the call stack; when it returns, it is popped — classic LIFO behavior.

recursion.question: What is the time complexity of a naive recursive Fibonacci implementation?
recursion.explanation: Each call branches into two sub-calls, leading to an exponential number of calls — approximately O(2^n).

recursion.question: Tail recursion is a special form of recursion where:

choices.B: The recursive call is the last operation before returning
choices.D: The base case is checked at the end

recursion.explanation: In tail recursion the recursive call is the final action, allowing compilers to optimize it into a loop (tail-call optimization).

hashing.question: What is the primary purpose of a hash function?

choices.B: Map a key to an array index

hashing.explanation: A hash function transforms a key into an integer index within the bounds of an array, enabling fast lookups.

hashing.question: A collision in hashing occurs when:

choices.A: Two different keys produce the same hash index
choices.D: The hash function returns a negative value

hashing.explanation: Since the hash space is finite, different keys can map to the same index — this is called a collision.

hashing.question: A good hash function should:

choices.A: Always return the same index for all keys
choices.B: Distribute keys uniformly across the table

hashing.explanation: Uniform distribution minimizes collisions, which is key to maintaining O(1) average-case performance.

hashing.question: The load factor of a hash table is defined as:

choices.A: Number of empty slots / total slots
choices.B: Number of stored elements / total slots
choices.D: Number of collisions / number of elements

hashing.explanation: Load factor = n/m (elements/slots). Higher load factors increase collision probability and degrade performance.

hash_tables.question: In separate chaining, collisions are resolved by:

choices.B: Storing colliding entries in a linked list at that index

hash_tables.explanation: Separate chaining maintains a linked list (or other container) at each slot, appending colliding entries to the list.

hash_tables.question: What is the average time complexity of lookup in a well-designed hash table?
hash_tables.explanation: With a good hash function and low load factor, the expected number of collisions per slot is constant, giving O(1) average lookup.

hash_tables.question: Open addressing resolves collisions by:

choices.B: Probing for the next available slot in the array

hash_tables.explanation: Open addressing (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing) searches for the next empty slot within the same array.

hash_tables.question: When should a hash table be resized (rehashed)?

choices.B: When the load factor exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.75)
choices.C: When the table is completely empty

hash_tables.explanation: Resizing when the load factor exceeds ~0.75 keeps collision rates low and maintains O(1) average performance.

trees_intro.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of a tree?

choices.C: Every node can have multiple parents
choices.D: There is exactly one path between any two nodes

trees_intro.explanation: In a tree, every node except the root has exactly one parent. Multiple parents would create cycles, violating the tree definition.

trees_intro.question: The height of a tree with only a root node is:
trees_intro.explanation: Height is the number of edges on the longest path from root to a leaf. A single root has no edges, so height = 0.

trees_intro.question: A leaf node is a node that:
trees_intro.explanation: A leaf node has no children — it is at the boundary of the tree.

trees_intro.question: If a tree has n nodes, how many edges does it have?
trees_intro.explanation: Every node except the root has exactly one incoming edge from its parent, so a tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges.

binary_trees.question: In a binary tree, each node can have at most:
binary_trees.explanation: By definition, a binary tree restricts each node to at most two children: left and right.

binary_trees.question: A full binary tree is one where:

choices.B: Every node has exactly 0 or 2 children
choices.C: All leaves are at the same depth

binary_trees.explanation: In a full (proper) binary tree, every internal node has exactly two children; no node has only one child.

binary_trees.question: A complete binary tree of height h has between ___ and ___ nodes.
binary_trees.explanation: A complete binary tree of height h has at minimum 2^h nodes (one node at the last level) and at most 2^(h+1)-1 nodes (all levels full).

binary_trees.question: The maximum number of nodes at level k of a binary tree is:
binary_trees.explanation: Each level k can have at most 2^k nodes (level 0 = 1 node, level 1 = 2 nodes, level 2 = 4 nodes, etc.).

tree_traversals.question: Which traversal visits the root node before its children?
tree_traversals.explanation: Preorder traversal visits root first, then left subtree, then right subtree (Root → Left → Right).

tree_traversals.question: Inorder traversal of a Binary Search Tree produces:
tree_traversals.explanation: Inorder visits left → root → right. In a BST, left < root < right, so the output is sorted ascending.

tree_traversals.question: Which data structure is used for level-order traversal?
tree_traversals.explanation: Level-order traversal processes nodes level by level using a queue to track the next node to visit.

tree_traversals.question: Postorder traversal visits nodes in the order:
tree_traversals.explanation: Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the root (Left → Right → Root).

binary_search_trees.question: In a BST, all keys in the left subtree of a node are:
binary_search_trees.explanation: The BST property requires that all keys in the left subtree are strictly less than the node's key.

binary_search_trees.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in a BST?
binary_search_trees.explanation: In the worst case (a completely skewed tree resembling a linked list), search must traverse all n nodes.

binary_search_trees.question: To delete a node with two children from a BST, you typically replace it with:
binary_search_trees.explanation: Replacing with the inorder successor (smallest in right subtree) or predecessor (largest in left subtree) maintains the BST property.

binary_search_trees.question: Inserting a sorted sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into an empty BST creates:

choices.B: A right-skewed tree (like a linked list)

binary_search_trees.explanation: Each new element is larger than all existing nodes, so it always goes to the right child, creating a linear chain.

balanced_bst.question: What problem do self-balancing BSTs (like AVL or Red-Black trees) solve?

choices.B: O(n) worst-case operations in skewed BSTs

balanced_bst.explanation: Self-balancing trees guarantee O(log n) height, preventing the O(n) degradation that occurs with skewed BSTs.

balanced_bst.question: In an AVL tree, the balance factor of every node must be:
balanced_bst.explanation: The AVL balance factor (height of left subtree - height of right subtree) must be -1, 0, or +1 for every node.

balanced_bst.question: Which operation restores balance in an AVL tree after an insertion?
balanced_bst.explanation: AVL trees use rotations (left, right, left-right, right-left) to restore balance after insertions or deletions.

balanced_bst.question: Red-Black trees guarantee that the longest path from root to a leaf is at most ___ times the shortest path.
balanced_bst.explanation: Red-Black tree properties ensure no path is more than twice as long as any other, guaranteeing O(log n) height.

heaps.question: In a min-heap, the smallest element is always at:
heaps.explanation: The min-heap property requires every parent to be ≤ its children, so the global minimum is always at the root.

heaps.question: A binary heap is typically implemented using:
heaps.explanation: Since a binary heap is a complete binary tree, it maps perfectly to an array: parent at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2.

heaps.question: The time complexity of extracting the minimum from a min-heap of n elements is:
heaps.explanation: The root is removed in O(1), but restoring the heap property (heapify/sift-down) takes O(log n).

heaps.question: Building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements takes:
heaps.explanation: Floyd's bottom-up heap construction algorithm runs in O(n) by sifting down from the last internal node upward.

sorting_basic.question: What is the best-case time complexity of insertion sort?
sorting_basic.explanation: When the array is already sorted, insertion sort only makes one comparison per element — O(n) total.

sorting_basic.question: Which of these sorting algorithms is stable?
sorting_basic.explanation: Insertion sort preserves the relative order of equal elements because it only shifts elements, never swapping distant equal elements.

sorting_basic.question: Selection sort works by repeatedly:

choices.B: Finding the minimum element and placing it at the current position
choices.D: Inserting each element into a heap

sorting_basic.explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum and swaps it into place at the beginning of the unsorted section.

sorting_basic.question: Bubble sort has a worst-case time complexity of:
sorting_basic.explanation: In the worst case (reverse-sorted array), bubble sort performs n(n-1)/2 comparisons and swaps — O(n²).

sorting_advanced.question: Merge sort's time complexity is:

choices.D: O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst

sorting_advanced.explanation: Merge sort always divides the array in half (log n levels) and merges in O(n) at each level — O(n log n) in all cases.

sorting_advanced.question: Quick sort's worst case occurs when:

choices.B: The pivot always splits the array evenly
choices.C: The pivot is always the smallest or largest element
choices.D: The array has only unique elements

sorting_advanced.explanation: If the pivot is always the extreme element, one partition has n-1 elements and the other has 0, giving O(n²).

sorting_advanced.question: What extra space does merge sort require?
sorting_advanced.explanation: Standard merge sort needs an auxiliary array of size n for merging, giving O(n) extra space.

sorting_advanced.question: Which sorting algorithm is typically fastest in practice for large random arrays?
sorting_advanced.explanation: Quick sort's cache-friendly in-place partitioning and O(n log n) average case make it the fastest in practice for most inputs.

graphs_intro.question: A directed graph differs from an undirected graph in that:

choices.B: Edges have a direction (from one vertex to another)

graphs_intro.explanation: In a directed graph, each edge goes from a source vertex to a destination vertex — the order matters.

graphs_intro.question: An adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices uses ___ space.
graphs_intro.explanation: An adjacency matrix is a V×V 2D array, requiring O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges.

graphs_intro.question: An adjacency list is more space-efficient than an adjacency matrix when:

choices.D: The graph is a complete graph

graphs_intro.explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space. When E << V², this is much less than the O(V²) matrix.

graphs_intro.question: The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is:

choices.A: The number of vertices in the graph
choices.B: The number of edges connected to that vertex
choices.C: The shortest path to the root
choices.D: The weight of its heaviest edge

graphs_intro.explanation: The degree of a vertex is the count of edges incident to it — how many direct neighbors it has.

graph_traversals.question: BFS explores vertices in order of their:

choices.B: Distance (number of edges) from the source

graph_traversals.explanation: BFS explores all vertices at distance k before any vertex at distance k+1, giving a level-by-level exploration.

graph_traversals.question: DFS can be implemented using:
graph_traversals.explanation: DFS uses a stack (explicitly or via the call stack in recursion) to track which vertex to explore next.

graph_traversals.question: The time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges is:
graph_traversals.explanation: Both BFS and DFS visit every vertex once (O(V)) and examine every edge once (O(E)), totaling O(V + E).

graph_traversals.question: To detect a cycle in an undirected graph, you can use:

choices.A: BFS or DFS — if a visited node is encountered again (not the parent)

graph_traversals.explanation: During BFS/DFS, if you encounter a previously visited vertex that isn't the current node's parent, a cycle exists.

shortest_path.question: Dijkstra's algorithm does NOT work correctly with:
shortest_path.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach assumes once a vertex is finalized its distance won't improve — negative weights break this assumption.

shortest_path.question: Dijkstra's algorithm uses which data structure for optimal performance?
shortest_path.explanation: A min-heap efficiently extracts the vertex with the smallest tentative distance, giving O((V + E) log V) complexity.

shortest_path.question: Bellman-Ford algorithm can detect:

choices.B: Negative weight cycles reachable from the source

shortest_path.explanation: After V-1 relaxation rounds, if any edge can still be relaxed, a negative cycle exists — Bellman-Ford detects this.

shortest_path.question: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph because:

choices.B: It visits nodes in order of increasing distance from the source

shortest_path.explanation: BFS processes vertices level by level, so the first time it reaches a vertex, it has found the shortest path (fewest edges).

tries.question: A trie stores characters of a key in:

choices.C: Individual nodes along a path from root to leaf

tries.explanation: Each node in a trie represents one character; a full key is represented by the path from root to a terminal node.

tries.question: The time complexity of searching for a word of length L in a trie is:

choices.A: O(n) where n is total words

tries.explanation: We traverse at most L nodes (one per character), regardless of how many words are stored — O(L).

tries.question: Tries are particularly efficient for:
tries.explanation: Tries share prefixes between keys, making prefix matching and autocomplete extremely efficient.

tries.question: The main disadvantage of a trie compared to a hash table is:

choices.C: High memory usage due to many pointers per node

tries.explanation: Each trie node may store up to 26 (or more) child pointers, leading to significant memory overhead compared to hash tables.

dynamic_programming.question: Dynamic programming is applicable when a problem has:
dynamic_programming.explanation: DP works when the same subproblems recur (overlapping) and optimal solutions can be built from optimal sub-solutions (optimal substructure).

dynamic_programming.question: Memoization is a DP technique that:

choices.B: Stores results of solved subproblems to avoid recomputation

dynamic_programming.explanation: Memoization caches the results of expensive recursive calls so the same subproblem is solved only once.

dynamic_programming.question: The bottom-up approach to DP differs from top-down in that it:

choices.B: Starts from the smallest subproblems and builds up iteratively

dynamic_programming.explanation: Bottom-up (tabulation) iteratively fills a table from the simplest subproblems to the full problem, avoiding recursion overhead.

dynamic_programming.question: The Fibonacci sequence computed with DP (memoization) has time complexity:
dynamic_programming.explanation: Each subproblem (F(0) through F(n)) is computed exactly once and stored, giving O(n) total time.
